findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile the response-size hypothesis against unreal-milky-sloth's RCA, which used the 219KB datum to REFUTE size as the transport-close cause (50KB failed while 219KB succeeded), before committing to size-bounding as the remedy for the transport close.
evidence: Plan: 'the same tool SUCCEEDED but returned 219,815 characters ... So the server can emit payloads far beyond what a client can absorb' — presented as support for cause 1 (Response size).

unreal-milky-sloth RCA comment: 'Rival: response-size limit / timeout — REFUTED. The failing list_tickets(open,epic) JSON-RPC line is 50,532 bytes. Claude Code succeeded on ~219,000 bytes — a payload ~4.3x larger. Size does not discriminate. The error is a serialization type error, not a size or timeout error.'
unreal-milky-sloth live-validation comment records ready_tickets returning 939,719 characters successfully post-fix — the transport-close symptom was the BigInt serialization defect, not size.
findings.finding: The plan treats the 219,815-character datum as CORROBORATING the response-size hypothesis, but the sibling ticket it cites (unreal-milky-sloth) already investigated this and REFUTES the size hypothesis using that same datum; the plan commits to size-bounding without reconciling with that prior investigation.
findings.location: Sections 'Corroborating datum from a different client' and 'Candidate causes' item 1
scenarios: Author invests in a size cap / pagination as THE fix for the transport close, when the sibling ticket's proven root cause (BigInt serialization emitting bare 19-digit numbers) is what actually closed the transport, and it is already fixed and live-validated.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a note in 'Candidate causes' acknowledging that the sibling BigInt ticket already refuted size as the transport-close driver, and scope this ticket's size-bounding work explicitly as a separate defensibility improvement rather than the fix for the observed 'Transport closed'.

findings.checklist_item: State a remediation branch (or hand-off) for each of the three candidate causes so the fix ACs are not silently coupled to only the response-size hypothesis.
evidence: AC: 'A large result is bounded — pagination, an explicit limit, or a documented cap'
The plan insists three causes are 'live and this ticket should not presume among them', naming BigInt serialization and a deploy cutover alongside response size
A bounding/pagination fix does not address a client-side BigInt serialization failure or an orphaned-session deploy cutover
findings.finding: The remediation acceptance criteria (bound the result via pagination/limit/cap; structured error) are wired only to candidate cause #1 (response size). If the evidence-based diagnosis lands on cause #2 (BigInt serialization) or cause #3 (deploy cutover orphaning sessions), the plan defines no remediation path for those outcomes, yet the LIVE-VALIDATION AC still gates closure on the symptom being gone.
scenarios: Diagnosis attributes the transport close to the 18:54:29Z container replacement orphaning live sessions — bounding results is a no-op
Diagnosis attributes it to BigInt out-of-range serialization in a JS client — size limits don't fix serialization
findings.suggested_fix: Split remediation ACs conditionally on the diagnosis: (a) if response size — bound + structured error as written; (b) if BigInt serialization — cross-link/hand-off to `unreal-milky-sloth` and define the serialization fix there; (c) if deploy cutover — cross-link `nemophilic-prettyish-cockroach` and scope this ticket to the structured-error + reconnect behaviour rather than size bounding.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the 'without pagination or a size guard' premise to reflect the existing lean-by-default projection on list_tickets (description/comments omitted unless full=True) and search's bounded results, and scope the bounding work to the paths that genuinely lack a cap (e.g. ready_tickets, and list_tickets full=True).
evidence: Plan: 'So the server can emit payloads far beyond what a client can absorb, and it does so without pagination or a size guard.'

src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:303-306 (list_tickets docstring): 'The list is **lean by default** — the bulky description and comments fields are omitted so a broad list stays small. Pass full=True for the complete ticket shape…'
src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:291,324: list_tickets has a `full: bool = False` parameter wired to rebar.list_tickets(..., full=full)
src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:371: search '…with bounded discovery results.'

The sibling ticket unreal-milky-sloth's own RCA already MEASURED response size as non-discriminating (50,532-byte failing list_tickets call vs a ~219KB succeeding call), which further undercuts the unbounded-size framing this premise supports.
findings.finding: The plan asserts the server emits large payloads 'without pagination or a size guard', but list_tickets already has a size-mitigation mechanism (lean-by-default projection dropping description/comments, with a full=True opt-in), and search advertises bounded results — so the blanket 'no size guard' premise is refuted for part of the surface it covers.
findings.location: Corroborating datum section: 'it does so without pagination or a size guard'; second Acceptance Criterion ('A large result is bounded')
scenarios: Author scopes the 'bound a large result' work as greenfield and re-implements a lean/limit path that already exists for list_tickets, or misses that ready_tickets (line 349) has neither a lean mode nor a limit — the real gap.
The size-cause candidate (#1) is pursued as if no guard exists, when list_tickets full=True is the only path that bypasses the existing lean default.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'without pagination or a size guard' with a scoped statement: list_tickets is lean-by-default (omits description/comments unless full=True) and search returns bounded results, but ready_tickets has no lean mode, no limit, and no pagination, and list_tickets full=True bypasses the lean default — those are the unbounded paths this ticket must cap.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an auth precondition to the LIVE VALIDATION criterion stating the deployed endpoint is OAuth-gated, that the validating client must present the configured OAuth bearer token, and that a 401/403 is a FAILED (not inconclusive) validation — mirroring the sibling ticket unreal-milky-sloth.
evidence: Plan says evidence 'must be OBSERVED against the deployed server at https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/mcp' but names no authentication step.

The sibling ticket that validates against the SAME endpoint (unreal-milky-sloth) carries an explicit 'Auth precondition' paragraph: the endpoint is 'behind the OAuth gate', 'The validating client MUST present the OAuth bearer token', and 'A 401/403 is a FAILED validation.'
T3 checklist item: 'Auth/HTTPS preconditions stated' — HTTPS is stated, auth is absent.
findings.finding: The mandatory LIVE VALIDATION step calls the OAuth-gated deployed endpoint but states no auth precondition; only HTTPS is stated, not the bearer-token/auth requirement.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — final 'LIVE VALIDATION — REQUIRED TO CLOSE' bullet
scenarios: A validator issues the live call unauthenticated, receives 401/403, and cannot tell whether that counts as a failed validation or an environment problem.
The live call is attempted from a session lacking a configured OAuth client entry, producing an opaque auth failure indistinguishable from the transport-close symptom the ticket is about.
findings.suggested_fix: Under the LIVE VALIDATION bullet, add: 'Auth precondition — that endpoint is HTTPS and OAuth-gated (see docs/mcp-auth.md / docs/mcp-client-setup.md); the validating client MUST present the configured OAuth bearer token, obtained from the existing local client entry and never echoed. A 401/403 is a FAILED validation, not an inconclusive one.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the structured limit error must reuse the existing `McpEnvelopeError`/`install_error_guard` envelope and that any bound should follow the existing `limit`-parameter convention, so no parallel error path or bespoke cap config is introduced.
evidence: Plan AC3: 'Exceeding any limit produces a STRUCTURED, actionable error, never a bare transport close.'

`src/rebar/_mcp_errors.py:37` `class McpEnvelopeError(RuntimeError)` and `:82` `def install_error_guard(mcp)` already re-raise a structured `error_envelope` for known rebar exceptions across all registered tools.
`src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:393` `def recent_session_logs(limit: int = 5)` shows an existing `limit` convention on this surface.
Sibling ticket `unreal-milky-sloth` fixed a related MCP-wire bug by reusing 'the same mcp.tool-rebinding seam as the existing install_error_guard' — precedent for extending, not rebuilding.
findings.finding: AC2/AC3 name a bounding limit and a 'STRUCTURED, actionable error' without noting the repo already ships a structured-error envelope (`McpEnvelopeError` + `install_error_guard`, `src/rebar/_mcp_errors.py`) and existing `limit` params (e.g. `recent_session_logs(limit=...)`); the plan should direct the fix to reuse/extend these rather than invent a parallel error path or a bespoke cap mechanism.
scenarios: Implementer writes a new size-guard error type / ad-hoc cap config instead of routing a limit-exceeded condition through the existing `McpEnvelopeError` guard, producing a second inconsistent error shape for MCP clients.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a note to AC2/AC3: 'the limit error is emitted through the existing `McpEnvelopeError` guard (`src/rebar/_mcp_errors.py`), and any bound reuses the existing per-tool `limit` parameter convention rather than a new config key.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Consider the MCP-native pagination convention (opaque `nextCursor` cursor tokens for list operations) as the prior-art baseline for bounding large `list_tickets`/`ready_tickets` results, and justify any ad-hoc limit/cap chosen instead of it.
evidence: Retrieved: MCP spec 'Pagination' (modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/server/utilities/pagination) — 'The cursor is an opaque string token, representing a position in the result set; Page size is determined by the server'.
Retrieved: Microsoft mcp-for-beginners and multiple guides describe cursor-based nextCursor pagination as the standard pattern for large tool/list results that blow the context/token budget.

Plan phrase: 'A large result is bounded — pagination, an explicit limit, or a documented cap — rather than emitted at unbounded size.' — offers an ad-hoc cap as an equal option without naming the protocol-native cursor convention.
findings.finding: The plan proposes 'pagination, an explicit limit, or a documented cap' as interchangeable bounding options without considering the MCP protocol's own first-class pagination mechanism (opaque nextCursor cursor tokens for list operations), which is the established prior-art answer to oversized list results.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, bullet 'A large result is bounded — pagination, an explicit limit, or a documented cap'
scenarios: Author implements a bespoke integer limit or hard cap on list_tickets/ready_tickets when an MCP-standard nextCursor pagination would interoperate with generic MCP clients that already understand cursors.
A cap silently truncates results, losing tickets, where cursor pagination would let a client page through the full set.
findings.suggested_fix: In the bounding acceptance criterion, name MCP's cursor-based pagination (opaque nextCursor) as the default candidate and require the plan to justify choosing a plain limit/cap over it — including how a plain cap avoids silently truncating tickets.
